newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan people ignore Deng's memorial service.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan people ignore Deng's memorial service.

text.p: Unlike their estranged countrymen in mainland China who stopped work and shed tears over paramount leader Deng Xiaoping's memorial service on Tuesday, the people of Taiwan went about their business without missing a beat.
As Deng himself might have feared, it was as if Taiwan's people considered the late patriarch a foreign leader and his death a foreign affair.
Traffic jammed Taipei's bustling streets, businessmen hustled from one skyscraper to the next and mothers took their toddlers for walks in city parks.
At a moment of funereal gloom for China, the only irregular aspect in Taiwan, regarded by Beijing as a renegade province, was the day's unusually sunny, warm weather.

At 10 a.m., when horns and whistles blew across the mainland in a dramatic three-minute salute to Deng, Taiwan was bathed in the ordinary sounds of daily urban life -- the only horns being those honked by impatient motorists.

None of the three state-run television stations and only one private channel broadcast live coverage of the eulogy to Deng delivered by China's president and Communist Party chief Jiang Zemin in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
In it, Jiang reaffirmed Beijing's determination to bring Taiwan back into what he called the embrace of the motherland.
"We must act in accordance with the teachings of Comrade Deng Xiaoping, striving to attain the objective of the motherland's reunification," he told mourners.
"The Taiwan question will be settled eventually and the complete reunification of the motherland will certainly be achieved," Jiang added.
Though China speaks of eventual peaceful reunification, it has threatened to attack the island should it try to declare independence.
Some Taiwanese said they viewed Deng's death as a positive development for China.
"Communist China will take a leap toward joining the democratic trend," said Hsu Su-hsing, a man in his 30s, near the Taipei train station.
Sixty-five-year-old Lin Jung said: "I hope Jiang Zemin can now improve China's economy."

Many on Taiwan still blame Deng for ordering war games and missile tests near Taiwan that rattled nerves in the run-up to the island's March 1996 presidential election -- the first popular vote for a Chinese leader in history.
China mounted the manoeuvres in what it acknowledged was a warning to Taiwan's people not to swerve from Taipei's longtime advocacy of reunification to pursue independence.
Taiwan and China split after Nationalist forces lost a civil war on the mainland in 1949 and withdrew to the offshore island.
Taiwan, ruled by the exiled Republic of China government, says it would agree to re-unify only after China adopts pluralist democracy and capitalism.
Despite warnings from political analysts that China may now suffer political instability, Taiwan people have remained aloof to Deng's passing.
"The leaders from both sides of the Taiwan Strait already have their ways of doing things, and this will not change with the death of Mr Deng," Chuang Chin-yi said.
Taiwan's volatile stock market, usually hypersensitive to political change, has soared since Deng died on Wednesday and hit a six-year high on Monday.
It fell off slightly on Tuesday but brokers attributed the drop to domestic factors rather than to worries over Beijing's memorial ceremony for Deng.
